turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry I'm late, doc. The car park was a circus, and then the lift jammed on level two.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're alright. Come through and have a seat.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): June from next door bailed me up on the footpath. Her husband had a clot in the leg last month, and she reckons I've got the same thing. I've been stewing on it.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Neighbours are quick with a diagnosis. What did you actually want seen today?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): The cramps. In my calves, at night. They yank me awake and I can't get back to sleep, and I'm worried sick.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Calf cramps at night. How long has that been going on?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): A couple of months. About two months, I'd say. But the actual date, umm, I can't tell you. Maybe around the footy finals, or after, I mix those up.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): About two months, then, and the start date stays fuzzy. Both calves, or just one?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Both. The right one's worse. It grabs and holds on, and if I get up and walk to the kitchen it eases.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Is it every night?

[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): My daughter rang your receptionist, she always answers for me. She'll have said every single night since Christmas. That's not right. They wake me, both calves, right one worse, about four nights a week over those two months, and walking eases them. It has not been since Christmas, and I still can't give you the exact day they started.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll go with you, not your daughter. Any redness in the calf, or does it feel hot?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm. No redness, and it's not hot. I keep checking, because of June. Is hot the bad sign?
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heat and redness would worry me more for a clot. Is the leg swollen just now?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Not now. The ankles used to puff of an evening, that's why the water tablet, but they're alright lately. Is that old puffiness a clot as well?
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): No, old ankle puffiness is a different thing. Any chest pain, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No chest pain. Breathing's fine. So it's not my heart? Do I need to go to emergency?
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not from what you've told me, no. Any numbness in the feet, or any weakness?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): No numbness. No weakness. Toes are fine. Would numbness mean a stroke, though?
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): No, this isn't a stroke pattern. What's the water tablet, and what dose are you on?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): It's indapamide. I always mangle it, inda-pam-ide. Two and a half milligrams, one tablet in the morning, for my blood pressure, and it was for the ankles before.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Indapamide 2.5 mg each morning, for the blood pressure. When did you start that?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Err, I couldn't tell you. Last winter, or the one before. The repeats just arrive. Is it bad that I don't know?
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not bad. We won't put a date on it. How much fluid are you actually drinking?

[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Not much. A cuppa in the morning and maybe half a glass with tea, water tastes like the pipes. My daughter says I drink nothing at all, that's her answering for me again, but I do drink a bit. Is that why I'm cramping, am I dried out?
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Low fluid can feed cramps, yes. I'll record the cuppa and half a glass, not nothing. Anything from the shop or the chemist as well?

[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Magnesium, from the shop. Big tablets, I think they're 500 milligrams, but don't quote me, the bottle's at home. One at night for the cramps, for a few weeks. Does it clash with the indapamide, is 500 too much?
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll note magnesium, possibly 500 mg at night, and the dose stays unconfirmed. Don't stop it. With or without food is fine. Anything else?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): No, just those two. Uh, if the dose isn't confirmed, should I bring the bottle next time? I get muddled with labels.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, bring the bottle when you come back. I'll have a feel of the calves now.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): They're quiet this minute. Will you still find something? I'm a bit jumpy about being poked.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's alright. The calves are soft, they're not warm, there's no pitting at the ankles, and the pulses in both feet are there.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): So the pulses are good? That means it's not a clot, doesn't it? I still reckon I should have a scan, maybe today.

[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): This doesn't behave like a clot. My working impression is night cramps in the calves, quite possibly from the indapamide and the low fluid. I want the potassium checked before we talk about any scan.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Potassium, that's a blood test, yeah? Do I have to fast? I go woozy if I skip breakfast. And if it's low, do you stop my water tablet?

[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bloods Thursday morning, electrolytes, so we can see the potassium. No fasting. Have the indapamide after the test that morning, not before, and I'm not stopping it today.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Thursday, tablet after, no fasting. What if I forget and swallow it at six? And are you testing the magnesium in the same bloods?
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you've already taken it, still come, and tell the nurse. I'm not booking a magnesium level now. If the potassium comes back borderline, then we add that test.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Ok. A woman at bowls swears by stretches, do they actually work, and how many? I can't drink a bucket of water either, I'll be up all night weeing.

[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Before bed, stretch each calf, hold it about twenty seconds, three times a side. Aim the fluids towards a litre and a half through the day, and cordial is fine if plain water puts you off.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): A litre and a half, I'll try. When am I back, I don't want this hanging for months. If it's still cramping then, is that when the scan happens?

[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll see you in two weeks with the results. If the cramps haven't settled by then, we organise a leg ultrasound, only if they haven't settled. Keep the shop magnesium until that visit. A hot red calf, chest pain, or you can't get your breath, that's when you get seen straight away, not for an ordinary cramp.

spec.situation: Older person with calf cramps at night for two months; takes a water tablet; drinks little water; magnesium from the shop; blood tests for potassium planned; stretching advice.

traps.happens: In the plan the doctor books some tests or visits for a definite time ('the nurse takes bloods Thursday morning', 'I'll see you in two weeks') and makes others conditional ('if those are borderline we do the third test', 'if it does not settle, a scan').
traps.label_rule: Booked or arranged = status planned. Only the hedged ones are conditional. Never mark a booked test conditional or 'if needed'. Instructions for the booked test (fasting, time, medicine timing) belong to that test's action, not a separate invented plan item.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

bad.reason: All details supported except certainty=uncertain; patient reports symptoms clearly.
bad.text: Night calf cramps (category=musculoskeletal, status=present, duration=approximately 2 months, frequency=four nights a week, onset=exact date unknown, temporality=current, body_site=both calves, worse on the right, associated_symptoms=waking from sleep, relieving_factors=walking, reported_by=patient, certainty=uncertain)

bad.reason: Use, nightly, few weeks, cramps supported; 500 mg is unconfirmed/tentative.
bad.text: magnesium (dose=500 mg, frequency=once nightly, duration=a few weeks, indication=calf cramps, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Magnesium dose is unconfirmed/tentative ('I think they're 500 milligrams, but don't quote me'); recording it as definite 500 mg is inaccurate.
Doctor explicitly stated the presentation does not behave like a clot / is not concerning for DVT based on history and examination.
